CHIEF COMPLAINT
Rash on face with residual symptoms.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient reports rash is doing much better with current treatment. She has a small amount of rash leftover. She was initially taking doxycycline twice daily and noticed significant improvement. One week ago, she reduced doxycycline to once daily on pharmacist's recommendation, thinking the rash was improving. However, after reducing to once daily, the rash has plateaued and is not continuing to improve. She stopped breastfeeding prior to starting doxycycline. She initially did not use elidel cream due to concerns after reading about it. Doctor clarified that risks she read about apply to oral high-dose long-term use in transplant patients, not to topical as-needed use. Current skincare regimen includes sulfacetamide wash twice daily and metro cream applied once daily after face wash. Patient denies using cetaphil cleanser, neutrogena wipes, or lotions. Physical exam reveals Fitzpatrick skin type IV, with a few faint erythematous papules on bilateral medial cheeks and mild redness around and underneath nostrils.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Patient reports feeling sun sensitive when outdoors and takes precautions with hat wearing. Denies facial dryness or skin thinning. Reports face feels good and moisturized after using sulfacetamide wash.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Perioral dermatitis, rosacea, including ocular rosacea.

MEDICATIONS
Doxycycline (currently once daily, to be increased to twice daily)
Sulfacetamide wash (twice daily)
Metro cream (once daily after face wash)

ALLERGIES
Not discussed.

FAMILY HISTORY
Not discussed.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient denies breastfeeding at this time. Reports sun precautions including wearing hat.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Fitzpatrick skin type IV. Bilateral medial cheeks with a few faint erythematous papules. Mild redness around and underneath nostrils.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Perioral dermatitis and rosacea, including ocular rosacia. Continue sulfacetamide wash once daily (reduced from twice daily to avoid over-drying). Continue metro cream once daily. Increase doxycycline to twice daily until rash resolves, then continue once daily for one week before stopping. Doxycycline may cause upset stomach, heartburn, and photosensitivity requiring sun protection. Tacrolimus ointment to be prescribed and applied to rash twice daily until resolved; may cause transient tingly or needle-like sensation but is not an allergy. Once rash resolves, discontinue tacrolimus and continue doxycycline for one week, then stop. Continue wash and metro cream. Elidel cream cancelled. Clindamycin removed from medication list. Patient advised to avoid steroids on face and to hold off on old products until follow-up visit. If rash begins to flare minimally, may try tacrolimus alone for a couple days; if not sufficient, restart doxycycline. Patient instructed to call or send MyChart message if rash worsens. Recommended basic moisturizer such as vanicream or petroleum jelly; samples to be provided. Advised to avoid anti-aging products and plant-based products; discussed need to inform provider before trying new products. Gently wash eyelids once daily with gentle cleanser such as vanicream; use Bruder mask as needed. Follow-up appointment scheduled for approximately four weeks.
